body: Licence plates in Brazil were white until 2018; now, a white plate with a blue stripe is used, with red plates for commercial vehicles.
Portuguese is spoken in Brazil, with unique features like -ão (vs. -ón), -ch (vs. -ll), and -nh (vs. -ñ) when compared to Spanish.
Most Brazilian soil is distinctly red, from light pink in Mato Grosso to deep maroon near Paraná river, but is not always red in the North East or Rio Grande do Sul.
Common Brazilian utility poles resemble a ladder at the bottom with rectangular segments and small holes near the top.
Most Brazilian road signs have black backs.
Blue road markers with road number and kilometre are seen on the sides of Brazilian roads.
Brazil uses yellow on black chevrons, unlike most of South America which uses black on yellow.
Most Brazilian roads have double yellow middle lines and white outer lines; single dashed yellow also occurs.
Brazilian roads frequently have white painted kerbs.
Many Brazilian houses have orange tiled roofs.
Transparent satellite dishes are common in Brazil and generally unique within Latin America.
Blue Fortlev water tanks are seen atop roofs throughout Brazil.
Generation 3 coverage in Brazil uses two types of cars: white with a stubby antenna (diagonal coil) or no antenna. The stubby coil can also be found in Ecuador, Colombia, and Mexico.
Generation 4 cars in Brazil show a visible front with blue, white/blue stripe, or white color patterns.
Brazil has Generation 4 smallcam coverage, lower-mounted cameras with circular blur at the front.
Most camera coverage in Brazil is along the eastern half, with sparse Amazon coverage; western roads are limited.
Area codes are frequent in Brazil and often use parentheses. Patterns are highly systematic by state.
Each Brazilian state has a two-letter acronym; these help identify state roads and are worth memorizing.
Postcodes (CEP) regularly appear on Brazilian street signs. The area is based on the first two digits, which spiral anticlockwise from São Paulo.
An elevation map of Brazil helps to learn where mountains exist; the southeast coast has the highest peaks.
Northeast Brazil is marked by dry soil, shrubs, and succulents (the Caatinga landscape), greener in rainy season.
The Amazon covers 40% of Brazil, mostly dense rainforest or grassy hills; roads are few and often remote.
Acre features small grass hills with sparse trees where roads run over them instead of around.
Rural Roraima is open plains with thin grass and large mountains in the background.
Rio Grande do Sul can be hilly or flat, with lush green fields; southern landscapes sometimes resemble Uruguay.
Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, and Espírito Santo often have rolling grassy hills.
Espírito Santo and its surrounds frequently have mountains with exposed rock.
Paraná pines with long horizontal branches and leafy ends can be found in the southern states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.
Coconut palms grow tall and thin, common in northeast and coast; also found in other regions worldwide.
Carnaúba palms have fan-shaped leaves and a smooth-to-spiked trunk, common in Ceará and nearby states.
Babassu palms with long, robust leaves grow throughout the Amazon and occasionally down the coast.
Açai palms are known for drooping leaflets and thin trunks, found around Belem and throughout the Amazon.
Moriche palms have round fan-shaped leaves and are most common in Amazonas, Acre, and Roraima.
Macaw palms feature thin leaves and a spear-shaped top; common in Mato Grosso do Sul.
Long-stemmed plants are frequent in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, and Paraíba, even visible in the dry season.
Very tall grass grows in Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia, and Minas Gerais.
Eucalyptus Grandis plantations are found throughout Brazil, especially in the south and Amapá.
Sugarcane plantations are most common in São Paulo and coastal northeast states.
Soybeans thrive mainly in Mato Grosso, Paraná, and Goiás.
Coffee beans are most common in Minas Gerais, and also in Espírito Santo and northeastern São Paulo.
Round concrete poles are common across southern Brazil, especially São Paulo, both urban and rural.
Wooden poles are used in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.
Pole supports connect crossbars to stems and vary by state. They're rare in the northeast.
Bahia and Pernambuco poles have long yellow paint with a black code; starts with a letter.
Goiás poles use long yellow paint with a black code starting with a number, or yellow on black.
Small yellow or orange plates appear high up on poles in Pernambuco, and lower in Rio Grande do Norte.
Pole IDs in Paraná use black paint with yellow or white painted text.
Most Maranhão poles have a small beige plate with numbers built into the pole surface.
Paraná utility poles at intersections sometimes have street names painted on them.
São Paulo's common poletop is an asymmetrical crossbar with a support to the longer bar.
Ceará and Rondônia have exclusive asymmetrical crossbars without supports; Rondonian ones are metal.
Ceará and Roraima poles feature a zigzag-shaped top bar, larger than normal electricity poles.
Pencil poles with a smooth cone top are found mostly in Rio de Janeiro, and rarely Brasília and Manaus.
Gamma-shaped poles with electricity boxes are common in Rio de Janeiro, Belém, Salvador, Fortaleza, and Maceió.
Electricity counters on poles are frequent in Cuiabá, Macapá, and major cities of Pará.
Poles with alternating horizontal insulators appear in Mato Grosso and southern Acre.
Brown mushroom insulators are unique to Pernambuco.
White mushroom insulators are found in Bahia, and rarely Brasília.
Transparent insulators are usually seen in Alagoas and Santa Catarina.
Insulators shaped like a spool of thread are frequent in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo.
Ceará sometimes uses long, thin insulators; rarely seen in Goiás.
Poles with horizontal insulators abound in Pará and less so in Mato Grosso.
Long grey insulators (not horizontal) are mostly in Pará, Mato Grosso, Tocantins, Bahia, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná, and Santa Catarina.
Black double UFO-shaped insulators in trident formation are common in Maranhão.
Cone/spherical 'lollipop' insulators are common in Rio Grande de Norte, Paraíba, and Pernambuco.
Dark brown insulators with grey bases are seen almost only in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
Concrete trash baskets are common in Acre and Rondônia (versus metal elsewhere).
Lamps in Minas Gerais and Goiás often feature two parts; also seen in other select states.
Lamps in urban northern Paraná may lack a lamp arm, appearing colorful and industrial or ornate.
Most poles in Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Pará, Amapá, Rio Grande do Norte, Pernambuco, and Santa Catarina have the lamp arm attached directly to the pole.
Lamps in Roraima are similar in style but differently colored in each major city.
Ceará lamps often have fancy and colorful arms with the town name.
São Paulo has the most divided highways of any Brazilian state.
Phone numbers are sometimes shown under kilometre markers in São Paulo.
Cobblestone pavement is mostly seen in northeast Brazil and Rio Grande do Sul.
Roads with hexagonal concrete tiles are more frequent in Santa Catarina and Minas Gerais.
Some roads in Acre use red brick.
Cobblestone roads with randomly sized stones are most common in southeast Rio Grande do Sul and Minas Gerais.
Uneven but mostly square stone roads are seen in west Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina; the soil nearby is very dark.
Brown tiled pavements with jagged or square patterns are common in Rio Grande do Sul, sometimes also Santa Catarina.
Buildings in southern Brazil, mainly Santa Catarina, are often of European-inspired design.
Wooden houses on stilts are common in Acre, more rarely in Amazonas and Pará.
Most roads in Piauí have red gravel on the sides; kerbs and tarmac are increasingly common.
Amapá’s Generation 4 coverage always has a camera smudge at the front right and uses a white car with a blue stripe.
Alagoas Generation 3 coverage can reveal rifts.
João-de-Barro nests, seen as spheres atop utility poles, are typical in Brazil’s south.
Around Uiramuta (Roraima), expect a dry landscape with folded mountains.
Coastal Rio Grande do Sul stands out as a rare flat wetland area.
São Paulo pole ID paint is square and yellow, with three letters, numbers, and a black line.
Campo Grande and Joinville street signs are stickers wrapped on poles at intersections.
Rio de Janeiro’s lamps have a curved arm throughout, not seen elsewhere.
Teresina lamps are usually blue with an orange arm.
Belém lamp heads are often orange.
Cuiabá lamps are usually light green, and may have poles with multiple electricity meters.
Lamps in Belo Horizonte and Uberaba in Gen 4 may have a white, numbered plaque.
Caxias do Sul lamps have zig-zag bent poles and yellow heads.
Florianópolis poles are painted white with blue and red stripes.
Northwest Rio Grande do Sul features a camera glitch in Gen 3 coverage.
BR-364 in Acre is recognisable for its rollercoaster-like hilly road, usually covered by Gen 3 with an antenna.
AM-319 crosses lush Amazon rainforest, mostly unpaved with bright orange soil, and features many wooden/ladder poles. Gen 4 blue car covers the stretch.
Pará's BR-163 is hilly, curvy, and dry with Amazon vegetation, heavily trafficked and Gen 4 blue car coverage.
Amazonian trekker coverage uses boat and walking routes through rainforest and villages near rivers.
Northeast Maranhão’s park has sand dunes with pools, covered by both truck and walking trekker.
Ilha de Fernando de Noronha is a Brazilian island 340km northeast of Rio Grande do Norte. It’s covered by white buggy and similar vegetation to the mainland, with boat coverage nearby.
